First, does the approach generalise to a pathogen whose surveillance signal is intrinsically weaker, as RSV positivity is relative to influenza positivity? Second, how sensitive are PINN-based R(t) estimates to parameters that the analyst fixes rather than estimates, in particular the recovery rate? Third, is laboratory positivity the right input at all, given that Hong Kong also reports age-stratified influenza-associated admission rates weekly?

This study addresses that gap using a single, well-characterised surveillance system in which influenza and RSV are measured by the same laboratory network over the same period, so that method performance can be compared across pathogens with minimal setting-level confounding. We evaluate four prespecified questions: (1) does R(t)-based onset detection generalise from influenza to RSV; (2) which signal characteristics determine method performance; (3) do age-stratified hospital admissions provide earlier detection than laboratory positivity; and (4) how sensitive are PINN-based R(t) estimates to the assumed recovery rate. The central contribution is negative in a specific and actionable way: across 18 pathogen-seasons, the apparent success or failure of R(t)-based onset detection was driven not by the sophistication of the estimator but by two things a surveillance agency can inspect in advance, namely the amplitude of the input signal relative to its off-season variability and the identifiability of the fixed parameters that convert transmission into R(t). We show that a low signal-to-noise input degrades both estimators in the same direction, that a single mis-specified recovery rate can convert an otherwise functional PINN into an apparent structural failure, and that age-stratified admission data supply lead time precisely on the seasons where positivity-based detection is weakest.

vd_moveTo: Materials and Methods
Data sources

Influenza surveillance data were obtained from CHP Flu Express weekly reports (https://www.chp.gov.hk accessed 15 March 2026; January 2014–March 2026; 638 weeks; 31 variables). Variables include laboratory positivity for H1N1pdm09, H3N2, and B (specimen counts and proportions from the Public Health Laboratory Services Branch); ILI consultation rates from sentinel private practitioners (ILI_PMP) and public family medicine clinics (ILI_FMC); influenza-associated hospital admission rates per 10,000 population for six age groups (0–5, 6–11, 12–17, 18–49, 50–64, 65+); school outbreak counts; A&E ILI rates; kindergarten and elderly care home fever surveillance; and severe case counts by four age groups. A data dictionary for all 31 CHP Flu Express variables (data_dictionary_flu_express.csv) is provided as supplementary material, including variable descriptions, units, sources, and coverage. Note that weekly specimen denominators (total specimens tested) are not published in CHP Flu Express and are therefore not available for this analysis.

RSV data were extracted from CHP weekly “Detection of other respiratory viruses” reports (641 weeks, 2014–2026) using a custom scraper (scrape_chp_respiratory.py, committed to the repository). The scraper extracted 641 weeks with no missing RSV_pct values, no duplicate year-week entries, and one temporal gap (May 2025). Forty-seven weeks had zero RSV-positive specimens. Five randomly selected weeks were identified for manual validation against published CHP figures (2015-W21, 2015-W35, 2019-W44, 2019-W52, 2022-W18); manual verification against the CHP website is pending. The influenza and RSV datasets derive from the same Public Health Laboratory Services Branch but are computed over different specimen sets with different referral and testing indications; multiplex testing practice also changed over the 2014–2026 period. This is the key comparability assumption of the cross-pathogen design and requires further evidence (e.g. comparison of weekly specimen counts for both streams) rather than assertion.

Weeks during January 2020 to December 2022 (157 weeks) were excluded from the primary influenza analysis due to near-zero activity under COVID-19 NPIs (mean positivity 0.68%). For RSV, only the 2020 season was excluded. Sensitivity analysis showed that including COVID-era weeks (2020–2022) in the non-season baseline reduced the threshold from 5.70% to 3.15% (due to near-zero positivity pulling down the mean), while restricting to 2014–2019 only raised it to 6.47%. Impact on post-COVID onset dates was 0–7 days across thresholds.
Season definitions

Six influenza seasons were analysed in the primary PINN evaluation: 2014/15, 2015/16, 2018/19, 2023 summer, 2023/24, and 2024/25. The 2016/17 and 2017/18 seasons were excluded from the primary PINN analysis due to multi-wave dynamics but were included in the admissions comparison (8 seasons total). For RSV, 10 seasons were defined spanning peak timing from February to December

. A supplementary table (Table S1) with exact start and end dates, peak timing, dominant subtype, and classification for all 18 seasons is provided (supplementary_table_S1_seasons.csv). Seasons were classified as single-wave or multi-wave using scipy.signal.find_peaks on 3-week rolling-mean smoothed positivity with prominence = 0.02 (minimum 2 percentage points above surrounding troughs) and distance = 8 weeks (minimum inter-peak separation). This procedure classified 2017/18 and 2023/24 as multi-wave (2 peaks each) and the remaining 6 influenza seasons as single-wave (script: final_supplementary.py).
EpiEstim R(t) estimation

The Cori et al. [2] Bayesian renewal equation framework was implemented in Python. Pathogen-specific serial intervals were used: mean 3.0 days (SD 1.5) for influenza [8] and mean 7.5 days (SD 3.5) for RSV [14] (Vink et al. 2014, systematic review estimating RSV mean SI at 7.5 days, SD 2.1 days; note that weekly data with a 7.5-day SI provides approximately one observation per generation, limiting temporal resolution).

A 4-week sliding window and uninformative Gamma(1, 0.2) prior were used. Weekly positivity was converted to pseudo-incidence counts by multiplying by 10,000 for positivity and 100,000 for admission rates. [Note: the Gamma(1, 0.2) prior is not scale-invariant; the different scaling factors for positivity and admissions affect the posterior, particularly at low denominators, and the degenerate R(t) maxima (~26,000) observed for some adolescent admissions runs are a symptom of this

. Demonstrating empirical scale invariance or using a consistent, justified scaling with a genuinely weak prior is required before the admissions-based lead times can be considered reliable.] Onset was defined as the first week with posterior mean R(t) > 1.0. A sensitivity analysis using CI-based onset (posterior 95% lower bound > 1.0) showed minimal difference from mean-based onset: median delay 0 days, range 0–21 days across 6 seasons, with 4 of 6 identical. The largest shift (21 days) occurred in 2015/16. Sensitivity was assessed across 20 SI/window configurations for influenza.

RSV SI sensitivity was assessed across 20 configurations (5 SI means × 4 window widths) on 3 test seasons. All configurations detected onset in every test season, with lead time SD of 9–12 days across configurations, comparable to the influenza SD of 8 days
. RSV onset detection was robust to SI assumptions despite the 7.5-day SI providing approximately one observation per weekly generation.
SEIR-PINN architecture

The PINN comprises a state network (4 hidden layers, 64 neurons, tanh activation) mapping normalised time t ∈ [0,1] to SEIR compartments via softmax (enforcing S+E+I+R = 1), and a parameter network (2 hidden layers, 32 neurons) outputting time-varying β(t) via softplus. The recovery rate γ was tested at three values: 0.1/day (10-day infectious period), 0.2/day (5-day, literature standard [8])

, and 0.33/day (3-day). R(t) = β(t)·S(t)/γ. Onset was defined as the first crossing of R(t) > 1.0 from below (requiring R(t) < 1.0 at some prior point) sustained for ≥3 consecutive evaluation points, after a 4-week burn-in. Training: 15,000 epochs, Adam optimiser, learning rate 10⁻³, StepLR scheduling (factor 0.5 every 3,000 epochs), gradient clipping at max norm 1.0. Random seed: 42. Single fit per season. Multi-restart analysis with 5 seeds (42, 123, 456, 789, 1024) showed stable results for 4 of 6 seasons

: onset date ranges of 7 days (2014/15), 20 days (2018/19), 15 days (2023 summer), and detection in 5/5 seeds for each. The 2015/16 season detected onset in 3/5 seeds, and the 2024/25 season had one outlier seed (onset 4 months later than the other 4). The 2023/24 multi-wave season remained unstable (3/5 detected, R(t) at burn-in crossing 1.0 in both directions). Full results at pinn_multi_restart_results.csv in the repository. Software: Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.2.2, on Intel MacBook Pro (no GPU acceleration).
Simulation study

Synthetic SEIR epidemics were generated with known β(t) (sigmoid onset, peak R₀ = 1.8) and parameters σ = 0.5/day, γ = 0.2/day. Observations were created under six scenarios: perfect I(t), scaled (c = 0.15), noisy (Gaussian SD = 0.005), delayed (2 time steps), filtered (moving average, kernel = 3), and detection-thresholded. R(t) was estimated with both fixed and free parameters.
Code is available at simulation_study.py in the repository (seeds: rep × 1000 + scenario hash;
50 replicates per condition; output: simulation_study_results.csv).
Pre-onset signal characterisation
Pre-onset amplification was measured as percentage change during 8 weeks before threshold crossing, averaged across 5 single-wave seasons

. Age-stratified onset was assessed using age-specific baselines (non-season mean + 1.96×SD). Non-season weeks were defined as those with positivity below the series median (excluding 2020–2022). Sensitivity analysis across multipliers (1.645, 1.96, 2.58) yielded thresholds of 5.21%, 5.70%, and 6.65% respectively, with onset date shifts of 0–7 days for most seasons. A Poisson-based threshold (95th percentile) yielded 3.30%, substantially lower. The threshold is also period-dependent: including 2023–2026 data raises it from 4.94% to 5.70%.

Published influenza estimates span approximately 2.2 to 3.6 days, from 2.2 days for A(H3N2) and 2.8 days for A(H1N1)pdm09 in a systematic reanalysis of household outbreaks [14] to 3.6 days (95% CI 2.9 to 4.3) in a Hong Kong household transmission study [16]; the value used here is central to that range rather than taken from a single estimate.

The influenza standard deviation of 1.5 days is likewise not taken from a single source; the nearest published value is 1.6 days, from the same Hong Kong household study [16]. The discretisation figures reported below are insensitive to this choice: the first weekly weight remains at or above 0.984 for standard deviations between 1.2 and 2.0 days.

Because the incidence series are weekly, each gamma distribution was discretised onto weekly bins, the first of which begins at 3.5 days, so that probability mass below that edge is dropped and the remainder renormalised. The serial interval available to the estimator is therefore not the one specified: for influenza, approximately 68.5% of the distribution falls below the first bin edge, the first weekly weight becomes 0.998, and the effective mean is 7.01 days; for RSV the corresponding values are 9.9%, 0.800 and 8.50 days (Supplementary Fig. S5). Under the exact week-lag distribution implied by weekly aggregation, approximately 57% of influenza transmission occurs within the same week and is unrepresentable in a renewal model that sets the zero-lag weight to zero; conditioned on a lag of at least one week, the binning used here is closer to that exact distribution than the alternative of left-aligned weekly bins (total-variation distance 0.004 against 0.011 for influenza, 0.052 against 0.244 for RSV). The limitation therefore applies to any renewal-equation analysis that discretises the serial interval onto the weekly grid, and methods that reconstruct daily incidence from temporally aggregated data before estimation are the available alternative [17,18]

The four seasons in which admissions led do not share an amplitude or a wave structure: +63 days (2024/25, the lowest-amplitude season at peak 10.5%), +42 days (2016/17, multi-wave), and +21 days each in 2014/15 and 2018/19, which are the second- and third-highest-amplitude seasons in the set at 38.6% and 30.0%.

The mechanism is specific, and it has two parts. Total infectiousness at a given week is a weighted sum over preceding weeks only, so when those weeks carry no admissions it is zero and the rate parameter of the Gamma(1, 0.2) prior becomes the entire posterior denominator. Where the current week is also empty, the posterior mean is 1/0.2 = 5.0; where it carries the first sustained admissions of the season, the posterior mean is (1 + ΣI)/0.2, which is the source of the reported maxima: all three affected channel-seasons satisfy this exactly, at 49,005, 26,005 and 27,505.

Where the current week is also empty, the posterior mean approaches 1/0.2 = 5.0, reaching it exactly in the two 12–17 year channel-seasons and 4.95 in the 6–11 year 2014/15 channel, where a single isolated admission six weeks earlier still contributes 0.0019 through the tail of the kernel. Where the current week carries the first sustained admissions of the season, the posterior mean is (1 + ΣI)/0.2, which is the source of the reported maxima: all three affected channel-seasons satisfy this exactly, at 49,005, 26,005 and 27,505, the preceding weeks contributing no infectiousness at the precision the implementation computes.

The last of these can be quantified: weekly discretisation removes approximately 68.5% of the specified influenza serial interval but only 9.9% of the RSV one, so the two pathogens are estimated with structurally different instruments and temporal resolution is confounded with amplitude. The direction of the difference does not favour resolution as the explanation, since the pathogen whose serial interval is more severely truncated is the one on which the estimator performs better.

This is a retrospective observational analysis of routinely collected, aggregated public surveillance data from the Hong Kong Centre for Health Protection. As all data are publicly available in aggregate form with no individual-level information, no ethics approval was required [to be confirmed with institutional review]. Reporting follows the RECORD guidelines for observational studies using routinely collected data and the EPIFORGE checklist for epidemic forecasting and modelling studies.

The study addresses four questions: (1) does R(t)-based onset detection generalise across influenza and RSV; (2) what signal characteristics determine method performance; (3) do age-stratified hospital admissions provide earlier detection than laboratory positivity; and (4) how sensitive are PINN-based R(t) estimates to the assumed recovery rate parameter.
